In that case the string is **Modifier**.

**Attributive role.** IF a disease mention is an unmarked prenominal noun-adjunct, not governed by a preposition, that directly precedes a head noun it characterizes (population, case set, patient group, study, series, risk, gene, or protein), THEN it is a **Modifier**.

**Modifier** is reserved for an attributive premodifier immediately preceding a non-disease head: a population, study, series, case set, cohort, patient group, risk, gene, protein, locus, or phenotype.

quotes.quote: A textual string may refer to two or more separate disease mentions. Such mentions are annotated with the **Composite Mention** category.

IF a coordinating conjunction joins two or more pre-head modifiers that together precede one unrepeated head noun within a single contiguous noun phrase, AND at least one modifier specifies an anatomical site, disease type, or pathological attribute, THEN label the full string from the first modifier through the shared head as one **Composite Mention**.

quotes.quote: Punctuation-separated disease lists remain under the list-based Composite rule in Section 2 (Example 7).

note: Section 2.1 shared-head rule excludes punctuation-separated segments; Section 2 list rule governs the whole string.

quotes.quote: **Disease Class**: Mentions that could be described as a family of multiple specific diseases (for example, an inheritance-pattern category such as "autosomal recessive disease").

quotes.quote: is annotated as **Specific Disease** rather than **Disease Class** when it refers to one individuated condition that the text is about.

A modifier that names a category shared by many diseases does not anchor the mention. An inheritance pattern such as "autosomal recessive" or "X-linked" narrows the class but does not pick out one condition, and it is not a subtype qualifier. "Autosomal recessive disease" in the example above therefore remains **Disease Class**.
**Do not apply this rule** when: the mention denotes a heterogeneous umbrella spanning multiple distinct etiologies, signaled by quantification, enumeration, or a set-denoting construction

quotes.quote: is annotated as **Specific Disease**, together with its prepositional complement or gloss, when the span is the name or definition of one disorder under any of the following: **(a) Identity alias, gloss, or appositive.** The span is introduced by a parenthetical, an appositive, or an alias marker ("so-called," "also known as," "also termed") and refers to the same condition as the named disorder. **Identity test:** substituting the named disorder for the span leaves the reference of the sentence unchanged.

note: Identity test is in Section 1.8(a), which the cited Section 1.1 omits.

This applies when either: a narrowing modifier anchors it to a single entity: an etiologic agent, a specific gene or locus, a specific organism, a specific anatomical site, or a subtype qualifier that picks out one recognized form of the disease (e.g., "classical" in "classical galactosemia," Example 15); or

quotes.quote: A disease mention is not labelled **Modifier** when it is the object of a preposition attached to a governing noun, such as a noun denoting history, risk, form, or the status of relatives or patients (e.g., "family history of …," "risk of …," "probands with …"). Such a mention is labelled: **Specific Disease** when it names a particular disease entity, including a fixed site-plus-category compound such as "ovarian cancer" (Section 1.6(iii)) or an abbreviation (e.g., "SLS" in "probands … with SLS");
quotes.condition_words: the object of a preposition attached to a governing noun

quotes.quote: **Argument role.** IF a disease mention is the head of its own noun phrase, the complement of a preposition or verb, or a clausal subject, THEN it is not a Modifier. It is **Specific Disease** when it names a particular condition, and **Disease Class** when it is a generic category term (Section 1.6).
quotes.condition_words: the head of its own noun phrase, the complement of a preposition or verb
